# Why this note exists {.unnumbered}

## What this note assumes

This note assumes familiar logarithms, expectations, PMFs, and PDFs. Before
the general measure definition, read

- [Measure and probability foundations](../Measure_Theory/measure-probability-foundations.qmd);
- [Lebesgue measure, absolute continuity, and Radon-Nikodym densities](../Measure_Theory/lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd).

If equation (1) still looks abstract, read the discrete formula and Bernoulli
example first, then return to it. The general equation says exactly the same
thing without restricting the distributions to be discrete or continuous.

Walker uses Kullback-Leibler divergence in two different spaces:

1. between a true sampling distribution and a candidate sampling model;
2. between two belief distributions on a space of candidate models.

The same measure-theoretic definition covers both [@kullback1951information].

# General definition {#kl-general-definition}

Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space. If
$P$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $Q$, written $P\ll Q$, then the
Radon-Nikodym derivative $dP/dQ$ exists and

$$
\boxed{
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\int \log\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}\right)dP
}.
\tag{1}
$$

If $P\not\ll Q$, define

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=+\infty.
$$

The order matters. Equation (1) averages under $P$, so it asks how costly it is
to use $Q$ when outcomes actually follow $P$.

“On the same measurable space” means that $P$ and $Q$ describe the same
possible outcomes and measurable events. The condition $P\ll Q$ means that
$Q(A)=0$ implies $P(A)=0$: $Q$ cannot declare impossible an event that remains
possible under $P$. The function $dP/dQ$ is the relative density explained in
the [Radon-Nikodym section](../Measure_Theory/lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#the-radon-nikodym-derivative-is-a-measure-level-density).

Throughout this note, $\log$ is the natural logarithm. Using base 2 changes
the numerical units from nats to bits but only multiplies KL by a positive
constant.

# Discrete formula

If $P$ and $Q$ have PMFs $p$ and $q$ on a countable set,

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\tag{2}
$$

Use the conventions

$$
0\log\frac0q=0,
\qquad
p\log\frac p0=+\infty\quad(p>0).
$$

The second convention expresses a support failure: $Q$ declares an event
impossible even though $P$ can generate it.

## A Bernoulli example

Let $P(X=1)=0.8$ and $Q(X=1)=0.5$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
&=0.8\log(0.8/0.5)+0.2\log(0.2/0.5)\\
&\approx0.193.
\end{aligned}
$$

Reversing the arguments gives a different value:

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)
=0.5\log(0.5/0.8)+0.5\log(0.5/0.2)
\approx0.223.
$$

# Density formula

Suppose both measures are dominated by the same measure $\nu$, with

$$
p=\frac{dP}{d\nu},
\qquad
q=\frac{dQ}{d\nu}.
$$

Then

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\,\nu(dx),
\tag{3}
$$

provided $P\ll Q$. For ordinary continuous densities, $\nu$ is usually
Lebesgue measure. For PMFs, $\nu$ is counting measure. The value in (3) does
not depend on which common dominating measure is used.

## Normal example

For $P=N(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2)$ and $Q=N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$,

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\log\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_0}
+\frac{\sigma_0^2+(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}
-\frac12.
$$

The asymmetry is visible: the variance of $Q$ appears in the denominator of
the mismatch term.

# Main properties

For probability measures $P$ and $Q$,

1. $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\geq0$;
2. $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$ as measures;
3. KL is generally not symmetric;
4. KL does not obey a triangle inequality;
5. KL can be infinite.

Therefore KL is a **divergence**, not a metric.

In the dominated case, nonnegativity follows from Jensen's inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
&=E_P\left\{\log\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right\}\\
&\leq
\log E_P\left\{\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right\}\\
&\leq\log 1=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The second inequality allows for $Q$-mass outside the support of $P$.

This proof is optional. Jensen's inequality says that applying a concave
(downward-curving) function such as $\log$ after averaging gives at least as
large a value as averaging after applying the function. The practical
conclusion needed later is simply $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\geq0$, with equality
only when the measures agree.

# Expected log score: the statistical interpretation {#kl-expected-log-score}

Suppose future data are generated from $P$ with density $p$, but we report
$Q$ with density $q$. The expected log score under the truth is

$$
E_P\{\log q(X)\}=\int p(x)\log q(x)\,d\nu(x).
$$

Expanding KL gives

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\int p\log p\,d\nu
-\int p\log q\,d\nu.
\tag{4}
$$

For fixed $P$, the first term does not depend on $Q$. Therefore

$$
\arg\min_QD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\arg\max_QE_P\{\log q(X)\}.
\tag{5}
$$

This—not the entropy prehistory—is the key identity for Walker.

# Parametric projection under misspecification {#kl-parametric-projection}

Let the true density be $f_0$ and let
$\{f_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ be a parametric family. The KL projection is

$$
\theta^*
=\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f_0\|f_\theta).
$$

Using (4),

$$
\theta^*
=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}
E_{f_0}\{\log f_\theta(X)\}.
$$

Under suitable regularity conditions, maximum likelihood estimation in a
misspecified family targets this KL-best approximation. This does not make the
family true; it identifies its best member under the log score.

# Walker's posterior decision problem {#kl-walker-decision}

Let $f$ denote a possible true density and $f_\theta$ a lower-dimensional
parametric action. Use utility

$$
u(f,\theta)=-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|f_\theta).
\tag{6}
$$

After observing data, maximize posterior expected utility:

$$
U_n(\theta)
=\int u(f,\theta)\Pi(df\mid X_{1:n}).
$$

By (4), the terms involving $\log f$ do not depend on $\theta$. Therefore the
same decision maximizes

$$
\widetilde U_n(\theta)
=\int\log f_\theta(x)\,P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}(dx),
\tag{7}
$$

where

$$
P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}(A)
=\int P_f(A)\Pi(df\mid X_{1:n})
$$

is the posterior predictive distribution.

There is a notation issue worth making explicit. On page 26, Walker first
prints the order $d(f_\theta,f)$, but the subsequent result (7) follows from
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|f_\theta)$, the order used in (6). The derivation, rather
than the preceding order of symbols, determines the required orientation.

# KL support in posterior consistency {#kl-support}

For a true density $f_0$, its KL neighborhood of radius $\varepsilon$ is

$$
K_\varepsilon(f_0)
=\left\{f:
\int f_0(x)\log\frac{f_0(x)}{f(x)}\,d\nu(x)
<\varepsilon
\right\}.
$$

The statement that $f_0$ is in the **KL support** of the prior $\Pi$ means

$$
\Pi\{K_\varepsilon(f_0)\}>0
\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.
\tag{8}
$$

Equation (8) says that the prior does not exclude every density that predicts
nearly like $f_0$ in expected log score. It is a support condition, not by
itself a universal guarantee of strong posterior consistency; additional
testing, complexity, or sieve conditions commonly enter consistency theorems.
Those proof terms are translated in the
[posterior-consistency note](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#support-is-important-but-not-the-whole-theorem).

# KL between belief distributions {#kl-belief-distributions}

Walker later compares a proposed posterior belief measure $\mu$ with a prior
belief measure $\Pi$. These measures live on the model space, not the data
space. If $\mu\ll\Pi$, define

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi)
=\int\log\left(\frac{d\mu}{d\Pi}(f)\right)\mu(df).
\tag{9}
$$

The functional

$$
\mathcal L(\mu)
=-\int\log L_n(f)\mu(df)
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi)
\tag{10}
$$

balances fit to data against departure from prior beliefs. Let

$$
\frac{d\Pi_n}{d\Pi}(f)
=\frac{L_n(f)}{\int L_n(g)\Pi(dg)}.
$$

Then direct algebra gives

$$
\mathcal L(\mu)
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi_n)-\log m_n,
$$

so (10) is uniquely minimized at the ordinary Bayesian posterior $\mu=\Pi_n$.
This is the variational argument developed in Walker's final section and later
generalized by Bissiri, Holmes, and Walker [@bissiri2016general].

Here a **functional** is a rule whose input is an entire probability measure
$\mu$ and whose output is a number. “Variational” means that the optimization
ranges over candidate distributions $\mu$, rather than only over a finite
parameter vector.

# Entropy is optional background

For a discrete distribution,

$$
H(P)=-\sum_xp(x)\log p(x)
$$

is entropy and

$$
H(P,Q)=-\sum_xp(x)\log q(x)
$$

is cross-entropy. Whenever the quantities are well defined,

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=H(P,Q)-H(P).
$$

This identity is useful, but entropy is not a prerequisite for using KL in
Walker. Expected log score and the Radon-Nikodym definition are the more direct
routes for statistical work.

# Common mistakes

1. Calling KL a distance without noting that it is not a metric.
2. Reversing $P$ and $Q$ without changing the interpretation.
3. Ignoring support mismatch and silently dividing by zero.
4. Comparing density formulas defined relative to incompatible reference
   measures.
5. Assuming small KL in one direction implies equally small reverse KL.
6. Treating KL support as sufficient for every type of posterior consistency.

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. When is $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)$ infinite because of support?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

It is infinite from support mismatch when $P$ puts positive probability where
$Q$ puts zero probability. Equivalently, $P\not\ll Q$: there is a measurable
set $A$ with $P(A)>0$ but $Q(A)=0$. With densities, this occurs when $p>0$ and
$q=0$ on a set having positive $P$-probability.
:::

**2. Under which distribution is the logarithmic ratio averaged?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Under the **first** distribution, $P$:

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\int\log\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}\right)dP.
$$

When both have densities relative to $\nu$, this is
$\int p\log(p/q)\,d\nu$. This asymmetry is why reversing $P$ and $Q$ changes
the decision problem.
:::

**3. Why does minimizing $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)$ maximize expected log score?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

If $Q$ has candidate density $q$, then

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\int p\log p\,d\nu-\int p\log q\,d\nu.
$$

The first term does not depend on $q$. Minimizing KL over $q$ is therefore
equivalent to maximizing $E_P\{\log q(X)\}$.
:::

**4. Which KL orientation produces Walker's posterior-predictive log-score
decision?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Use $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|q_\theta)$: the unknown candidate density $f$ is first
and the action density $q_\theta$ is second. Averaging
$-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|q_\theta)$ under the posterior leaves the
$\theta$-dependent criterion

$$
\int\log q_\theta(x)P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}(dx).
$$

The reverse orientation generally does not reduce to this posterior-predictive
expected log score.
:::

**5. In (9), do $\mu$ and $\Pi$ live on data space or model space?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

They both live on **model space**: they are probability measures on the
measurable space of candidate densities or distributions. In
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi)$, the first measure is a candidate updated belief
distribution and the second is the prior. The observed data enter through the
likelihood term, not as the points integrated over in this KL divergence.
:::
